## Conclusion

No, on both of the two goals the appropriation set for itself: 120 of a planned 300 beds opened, and unsheltered counts fell 6 percent against a 15 percent target [1][2]. The auditor attributes the shortfall to capital-project delay rather than to spending outside the appropriation, and found expenditures consistent with the allowed uses [1]. The strongest opposing view is that measuring a two-year programme against its own launch-year targets scores the forecast rather than the programme, and that shelter utilization of 94 percent is evidence the beds that did open were the binding constraint rather than the strategy [2][4] — that reading is defensible on the record and is why this report separates "missed its targets" from "did not work". Against the stated goals, the answer is no; against a counterfactual nobody measured, the record does not say.

## Key findings

- The adopted fiscal 2023 budget raised homeless services funding by 40 percent, with stated goals of 300 additional shelter beds and a 15 percent reduction in unsheltered counts within two years [3][5].
- The program office spent $4.1 million of the $6.2 million increase in the first year and opened 120 of the planned 300 beds [1].
- The auditor found expenditures consistent with the appropriation's allowed uses but execution roughly nine months behind the published schedule [1].
- The 2025 point-in-time count recorded a 6 percent reduction in unsheltered homelessness against the 15 percent goal [2].
- Shelter utilization averaged 94 percent of available beds across the period, indicating demand exceeded the capacity actually delivered [4].

## The strongest counterargument

The strongest case against a negative verdict is that the targets were a forecast, not a standard. They were set before the appropriation was spent, by the office that requested it, on assumptions about construction timelines that two seismic retrofits invalidated [1]. The council resolution that adopted them fixed the two-year horizon at the same time, before any of those assumptions had been tested [5]. Judging the programme against them measures the quality of that forecast. The counterfactual question — how many people would have been unsheltered in 2025 with no increase at all — is the one a resident actually cares about, and no document in the record answers it.

The utilization figure gives that objection real force: at 94 percent occupancy the beds that opened were full, which is consistent with capacity rather than strategy being the binding constraint [4]. What would have to hold for the conclusion to flip is evidence that the 180 undelivered beds would have converted into unsheltered-count reductions at the assumed rate — plausible, but unmeasured, and the count's own methodology change cuts in the same direction without settling it [2]. The verdict above is therefore stated against the goals the appropriation set, which is the question asked, and is explicitly not a finding that the spending was wasted.

## Spending and execution

The program office squandered much of the new appropriation on a boondoggle of an outreach initiative, spending $4.1 million of the $6.2 million increase in the first year while opening only 120 of the planned 300 beds [1]. The auditor's review found expenditures consistent with the appropriation's allowed uses but execution roughly nine months behind the published schedule [1].

Capital delays accounted for most of the shortfall: two of the three planned shelter conversions required unanticipated seismic retrofits, adding both cost and time [1]. Neither retrofit was foreseeable from the condition assessments available when the budget was adopted [3].

## Outcomes

The 2025 point-in-time count recorded a 6 percent reduction in unsheltered homelessness against the 15 percent goal [2]. Counting methodology changed between the 2023 and 2025 counts, which the count administrators note may understate the true reduction by one to two percentage points [2].

Shelter utilization averaged 94 percent of available beds over the period [4]. Occupancy at that level is generally read as demand exceeding delivered capacity rather than as capacity exceeding need.

The two outcome measures are not independent. Beds that did not open cannot reduce an unsheltered count, so the capacity shortfall in [1] and the count shortfall in [2] are partly the same fact reported twice. How much of the 9-point gap against the reduction target the missing 180 beds would have closed is not estimated in either document.

## Assessment

Measured against its stated goals, the programme fell short on both capacity and unsheltered reduction at the two-year mark, while the auditor found no misuse of funds [1][2]. The dominant cause identified in the record is capital-project delay rather than spending outside the appropriation [1].
